passage: Counselling note, Tuesday. Vikas came in because his friend Deepak stopped replying three weeks ago, without a word. He said he felt confused and small, and he kept checking his phone during our talk. He told me he had sent many messages and had not stopped rereading the last ones. We talked about how someone's silence can be about their own reasons, not about Vikas's worth. I did not tell him what Deepak thinks, because I do not know. He said the hardest part is never getting an answer. We agreed that he would stop sending messages for now, leave the phone in his bag at cricket practice on Saturday, and come back next week to tell me how it went. I will check in then.

qa.q: How long ago did Deepak stop replying?
qa.a: Deepak stopped replying three weeks ago.

qa.q: What did Vikas feel, and what shows it?
qa.a: Vikas felt confused and small, and he kept checking his phone and rereading the last messages.

qa.q: What did Vikas and the counsellor agree that he would do next?
qa.a: Stop sending messages for now, leave the phone in his bag at cricket practice on Saturday and come back to report.

qa.q: Why did the counsellor avoid saying what Deepak thinks?
qa.a: The counsellor does not know Deepak's reasons, and guessing could pull Vikas further into chasing answers.

grounding: A person is ghosted, feels confused and small and accepts he may never get answers instead of chasing.

passage:
Day 1: Aditi, who had messaged Himani every night for a month since they met at the book club, stopped replying mid-conversation. Himani's last message, "haha same! coffee saturday?", sat there unanswered.
Day 4: Himani had typed and deleted six messages. "Did I say something?" "Are you okay?" "Hello??" In the end she sent just one: "Hope you're alright. The coffee offer stands." Then she made herself put the phone in a drawer for the evening. She felt small and stupid, replaying every joke she'd made.
Day 20: Still nothing. Walking home from book club, Himani told her friend Tsering, "I keep thinking it was me." Tsering said, "Maybe Aditi just couldn't say whatever it was. Either way, you did nothing wrong by being friendly." That night Himani archived the chat. She didn't delete it. She just stopped opening it.

qa.q: What was Himani's last message before Aditi stopped replying?
How did Himani feel on Day 4?
qa.a: Small and stupid, replaying every joke and wondering what she had done wrong.
Sending one kind message instead of six, putting the phone away, talking to Tsering, and archiving the chat.

qa.q: How does Tsering see Aditi's silence?
qa.a: As likely about Aditi's own difficulty in saying something, not proof that Himani did anything wrong.

grounding: Shows being ghosted and feeling small, then accepting there may be no answer and that the silence says more about the other person.

passage:
Vaibhav, beta, you keep checking your phone. Someone stopped replying? Let me, your Binita pishi, tell you a story from before phones.
In 1985 I was twenty, in Shillong, writing every week to a boy called Arun whom I'd met at a cousin's wedding. For six months he wrote back, long letters with pressed leaves inside. Then nothing. I wrote three more letters. Then a fourth, angry. Then I walked to the post office every day for a month, asking the postman if something had got lost.
I decided I'd been too boring. Too forward. Too something.
Years later a friend told me Arun had simply got engaged and hadn't known how to tell me. So he told me nothing. It had nothing to do with my letters.
I wish I had stopped at the first unanswered letter and kept my own peace. His silence was about his courage, not my worth. So, beta, put the phone down and come and eat. Your pishi has made luchi.

qa.q: What did Arun put inside his letters?
How did Binita feel about herself when the letters stopped?
qa.a: That she had been too boring or too forward; she felt small and blamed herself.

qa.q: What does Binita wish she had done?
qa.a: Stopped at the first unanswered letter and kept her own peace, instead of writing more and asking the postman every day.
He had got engaged and didn't know how to tell her, so he said nothing.

grounding: Illustrates being ghosted, the urge to chase and self-blame, and learning that the other person's silence was about them, not one's worth.
